was surprised to see so much panic today, likely made worse by other things like rates and oil that distorted the actual substance in the AI/math talks

tl;dr — you're all gonna be fine. the leading chains of today have ample means to be able to respond to something like this in the unlikely scenario of it happening

longer:

i) is AI getting better at math? yes

does that imply that it will suddenly shatter foundational cryptography concepts? no

"computer smart. therefore the past work of all mathematicians is probably wrong." is not a logical chain with basis

sure, AI will find flaws in past human work in many areas -- in the same way humans themselves find flaws from other humans in many areas. this is how science works

if we find issues, we discuss them, fix them, and evolve

it takes large leaps of complete doomerism to assume that all teams, individuals, and ecosystems will fail at literally everything ranging from planning to prediction to detection to mitigation on all time horizons simultaneously

further, in these scenarios, AI is exclusively seen as a tool *only* for max destruction but never as a thing capable of a solution

so, it can apparently break everything but not fix anything. i hope you can see the bias here

for one, we already know this to be false given recent scaling of formal verification via ai 

it is of course easier for AI to make progress in fields and topics that are relatively less looked at vs something like foundational cryptography which all intelligence agencies, nation states, and high-level mathematicians are heavily incentivized to break, all the time

ii) the most unhinged doomsday scenarios assume an instantaneous attack with no lead time by a random person outside of law and jurisdiction, which I would posit is simply not possible

even ignoring the fact that the labs would get there first (and hence the government)

it's not as if one can just break all cryptography on all chains via their beefed up cloud hosts over a few hours or days or even months 

that not only assumes an algorithmic advancement with unfathomable magnitudes of improvement but also completely ignores the gargantuan operational complexity and opportunity cost of doing a global heist (vs the trillion other more important things you can do with an ECC break) 

it would be vastly impressive if a slight speedup could be found, but the speedups required to fulfill the doomsday fantasies of people on here are not grounded in anything

iii) importantly, assume I am completely wrong for all of the above

well even in that case, upgrading the systems in a world where ECC breaks is entirely possible and feasible (and has been worked on for decades)

in fact, there are many ways of doing it that we know of depending on the existing constraints of the system! 

imo, the biggest "risk" in all this is that a frontier lab publishes something about a slight speedup in the future, and then everyone extrapolates that to default to panic which then leads to a selloff like today

I don't think this is all bad because it never really hurts to think about and plan for these things on the protocol level, but the "retail" panic was certainly a huge self-own by the people pushing this stuff

doomerism is not going to win in crypto

Hard to overstate how much better you can sleep with the safety/security of TradFi for the vast majority of portfolio.

Smart contracts have been live on Ethereum for 11 years.

& on their own, they still can't read a webpage.

Everything they know has to be fed to them as a clean number. Prices. Timestamps. Balances.

The real world is messier. News articles, PDFs, agreements written in English, two sources that disagree.

That's the gap @GenLayer built Intelligent Contracts for.

𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐝𝐨

• fetch & read live web pages
• process text, PDFs & images
• follow rules written in plain English
• use AI to judge outcomes that aren't a simple yes or no
• settle the result on-chain

𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐲 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭

• 5 random validators check each result
• each one runs a different model or config
• majority rules
• appeal it & the panel jumps to 11, then 23, then 47
• around 30 minutes in the normal case

The clever bit: two answers can be worded differently & still count as the same answer. The developer decides what "equivalent" means. That's how a group of different AIs reach agreement.

• prediction markets resolved from live news
• insurance that pays out on flight delays & droughts
• escrow between AI agents that checks the work was actually done
• marketing deals where brands only pay for real results
• oracles that settle questions instead of trusting one data provider

The agents are coming either way. They'll need contracts that can read.

The market is selling off on “news” that is barely news.

OpenAI reportedly told investors that its annualized revenue was approaching $50B at the end of September, rather than the ~$70B figure that was widely reported last month.

But the gap largely comes down to accounting methodology, not a $20B hole in OpenAI’s business.

Anthropic counts revenue generated through cloud partners such as AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI apparently does not. Investors had therefore adjusted OpenAI’s reported figures to make them comparable with Anthropic’s, which helped produce the ~$70B estimate.

So we are essentially talking about whether revenue flowing through cloud partners is included in the headline number or not.

That is a comparability issue, not some sudden collapse in OpenAI’s revenue trajectory.

The fact that the market is treating this as a major negative for AI is, frankly, pretty ridiculous.

Over long periods of time, debts tend to rise faster than incomes, creating the long-term debt cycle.

Even as people become more indebted, lenders freely extend credit because during economic booms, incomes rise, asset values soar, and the stock market thrives. People borrow more to buy financial assets, pushing prices higher and creating a bubble.

So long as incomes keep rising, the debt burden stays manageable. But this cannot continue forever. Over decades, debt burdens slowly accumulate until debt repayments grow faster than incomes. This forces people to cut back on spending, causing incomes to fall and borrowing to dry up—eventually reversing the entire cycle.

David Sacks: The Economy Is Stronger Than You Think

“There's been a tremendous amount of economic data in just the last week or two showing that the economy is much stronger than people are giving it credit for.

So first of all, Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%, so that's basically a 50% increase. Economists had expected no revision. Q1 was also revised up to 2.5% from 2.1%. And if you look at the Q3 growth, it's tracking well above that. The Atlanta Fed GDPNow is showing around 3.7% as of late last week.

And then there was also some good news on inflation, we saw that core PCE just came in at 3.0% versus 3.3% expected. So inflation is still a bit too high, but actually it is cooling and beating expectations.

And then finally, you look at manufacturing. We're seeing a huge wave of re-industrialization in this country. A couple of the measures are the Chicago PMI and then ISM Manufacturing. They both are well into expansion territory and beating forecasts.

Just one last point, let's talk about poverty for a second, because I want to address the idea that this is just a K-shaped recovery.

So if you look at US household income, it's now at record high. The median household income is almost $90,000, and after-tax household income is growing again in the second Trump term, it's averaged 3.1% a year. In Trump 47, it was 3.9%, in Trump 45, and it was -1.2% in Biden's term as a four-year average. So we're seeing that after-tax household incomes have risen by 3.1%, and the poverty rate in the US has fallen to its lowest level in history, 10.2%.

So the poverty rate, the child poverty rate, these are all at historic lows. The average household's real income after inflation, after taxes, is increasing for the first time in years.

And you've got this SI boom that the Wall Street Journal said is bigger than the railroads, the canals, and the electric grid combined, and all these things are basically fueling strong growth in the economy.

And again, I would just dispute the K-shaped narrative because the poor are benefiting and the average household are benefiting as well.”

Jason Calacanis: Everyday Americans Need to Benefit From the AI Boom

@Jason on the Super Intelligence Summit at the White House:

“Awesome to see the power of all these American industries together.

I think the next piece of this puzzle is to start to include Americans in this, the bottom half of the K-shaped recovery.

Where's the teacher? Where’s the teenager going into college in all of this? Where's the American tool belt worker, the plumber?

It looks from the outside, I think, to a lot of Americans that this is still a bit scary, so there's more work to do there.

I was on a flight on Delta, and the flight attendants asked me what I did, and I was talking to them and they said, ‘I'm so scared of this AI stuff. I'm so glad I'm retiring because I don't want to lose my job.’

Americans are still petrified of this technology. They still think they're losing their jobs. They still think it's dangerous.

So I thought this was a great first step, but there's more work to do to pull Americans back off that ledge.

And we need to, and I think this is where the president or the next president could have a really major impact, is to start forcing American companies to not just think about how they make more money, how they get more green lights for their data centers, how they get less regulation and more free markets, but how does this lower the cost of education? How does this build more homes? How does this help healthcare? How do people get more healthcare at a lower price? None of that was addressed.”
